findings.claim: Question types labelled '4 marks — Describe Two Features', '8 marks — Explain Causation', '10 marks — Explain Two Reasons', '16 marks — Significance Question' and '18 marks — Depth Study Essay'; the two-feature mark scheme also awards 2 marks per feature.
findings.truth: The non-British depth study section carries 40 marks in four or five questions: a 2-mark 'Describe', a 10-mark 'Explain' on second-order concepts, a source question worth 10 marks or two source questions worth 5 marks each (always two sources), and an 18-mark essay. There is no 4, 8 or 16-mark question, and no SPaG marks in this section (SPaG attaches to question 4 of the period study and question 2 of the British depth study).
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md assessment tables for the non-British depth study; SPaG allocation in the assessment section

findings.claim: “In an ‘explain two reasons’ question ... Examiners want identification, detail and consequence: all three in every point.”
findings.truth: 'Explain two reasons' is another board's question form, and the claim about what examiners want is invented. The explain question here is a single 10-mark 'Explain...'.
findings.evidence: spec assessment tables; no source for the examiner claim

findings.claim: “Examiners expect you to distinguish McCarthyism ...”
findings.truth: An invented claim about examiner expectations. The advice itself is sound; the attribution is not.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: Welch quoted as “Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?”
findings.truth: The transcript reads: “Have you no sense of decency, sir, at long last? Have you left no sense of decency?” The clause ‘at long last’ belongs to the first question.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Joseph Nye Welch' (Army-McCarthy hearings, 9 June 1954)

findings.claim: 'civil liberties' defined as “A system of government that protects individual rights and freedoms”
findings.truth: Civil liberties are the rights and freedoms themselves, not a system of government. A student using this definition would define the wrong thing.
findings.evidence: standard definition

findings.claim: “Examiners reward specific examples over generalised statements ...”
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: “Poll taxes, literacy tests and white primaries prevented registration”, given as the position in the late 1940s and early 1950s.
findings.truth: The Supreme Court struck down the white primary in Smith v Allwright (1944). Southern states evaded the ruling until Terry v Adams (1953), so by the late 1940s the white primary was already unconstitutional and cannot be listed alongside the poll tax as a working legal bar.
findings.evidence: Smith v Allwright (1944); Terry v Adams (1953)

findings.claim: “Examiners reward complexity on Rosa Parks”
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: “Examiners will reward students who understand that non-violence was a deliberate strategic choice ...”
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: “boycott began 1 December 1955 and ended in victory November 1956”; a flashcard also dates the end of the boycott to November 1956.
findings.truth: 1 December 1955 is the date of Rosa Parks's arrest. The boycott began on 5 December 1955 and ended on 20 December 1956, when the Browder v Gayle order (decided 13 November 1956) reached Montgomery and the buses were desegregated.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Montgomery bus boycott'

findings.claim: “Examiners reward students who can distinguish ...”
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: Bloody Sunday at Selma described “as cameras broadcast the scene live on national television”
findings.truth: The attack on 7 March 1965 was filmed, not broadcast live. ABC interrupted its Sunday evening film that night to show the footage, which is what produced the national outrage.
findings.evidence: standard accounts of the 7 March 1965 broadcast

findings.claim: “Birmingham, March on Washington and Selma — how mass protest forced the Civil Rights Act 1964.”
findings.truth: Selma came in March 1965, after the Civil Rights Act, and led to the Voting Rights Act 1965. The description puts an event after the law it is said to have caused.
findings.evidence: chronology within the lesson itself

findings.claim: “Examiners expect you to present the Black Panthers accurately ...”
findings.truth: An invented claim about examiner expectations.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: COINTELPRO “revealed by the Church Committee Senate investigation in 1975”, repeated in the key fact box, the conclusion and a flashcard; and “COINTELPRO's methods were declared illegal by the Church Committee.”
findings.truth: COINTELPRO became public on 8 March 1971, when the Citizens' Commission to Investigate the FBI burgled the Media, Pennsylvania field office and leaked the files to the press. Hoover shut the centralised programme down within weeks. The Church Committee investigated in 1975–76 and condemned it, but it did not reveal it, and a Senate committee cannot declare anything illegal.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'COINTELPRO'

findings.claim: “Examiners reward students who identify the limits of legislative gains ...”
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward.
findings.evidence: no source

findings.claim: “the American Indian Movement (AIM) was founded in Minneapolis by Dennis Banks and Russell Means”, repeated in a knowledge check stem and a flashcard.
findings.truth: AIM was founded in Minneapolis in July 1968 by Dennis Banks, Clyde Bellecourt and George Mitchell (with Eddie Benton-Banai). Russell Means joined in 1969 and became the movement's best-known spokesman, but he was not a founder.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'American Indian Movement'

findings.claim: “AIM, founded in 1968, organised the Alcatraz occupation (1969–71)”, and the knowledge check matches the Alcatraz occupation to AIM.
findings.truth: The November 1969 occupation of Alcatraz was organised by Indians of All Tribes, led by Richard Oakes. AIM members took part but AIM did not organise it; AIM led the Trail of Broken Treaties and Wounded Knee.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'American Indian Movement'

findings.claim: “Rudolfo ‘Corky’ Gonzales”
findings.truth: His name is Rodolfo ‘Corky’ Gonzales.
findings.evidence: standard spelling

findings.claim: “The Church Committee later documented FBI surveillance of AIM as part of broader COINTELPRO-style operations.”
findings.truth: FBI surveillance of AIM is well attested, but the Church Committee's published case studies did not cover AIM, and AIM post-dates most of COINTELPRO. The attribution is unsupported rather than demonstrably false, and it costs no marks.
findings.evidence: Church Committee final report contents

findings.claim: “For Nixon, examiners want you to assess his welfare record fairly” and “Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974, the first US president to do so.”
findings.truth: The examiner claim is invented. Nixon is the only US president to have resigned, not the first; the lesson text and the knowledge check both say 'only'.
findings.evidence: no source for the examiner claim; internal contradiction on 'first'

findings.claim: “In May 1970, Nixon announced the expansion of the war into Cambodia.”
findings.truth: Nixon announced the Cambodian incursion in a televised address on 30 April 1970. The date matters because the campus protests, and then the Kent State shootings of 4 May 1970, followed within days.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the Cambodian campaign

findings.claim: “His vice president, Gerald Ford, issued a pardon.”
findings.truth: Ford became president on 9 August 1974 when Nixon resigned, and pardoned Nixon on 8 September 1974 as president. A vice president cannot issue a pardon.
findings.evidence: US Constitution, Article II; the pardon of 8 September 1974

findings.claim: “Nixon also signed the Environmental Protection Agency into existence (1970)”, and the mark scheme says he “signed the Environmental Protection Agency into law (1970)”.
findings.truth: The EPA was not created by an Act of Congress. Nixon created it by a reorganisation plan that took effect on 2 December 1970.
findings.evidence: Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1970

findings.claim: The lesson teaches Watergate, the Pentagon Papers and Nixon's resignation at length, and one practice question is wholly about Watergate.
findings.truth: Neither Watergate nor the Pentagon Papers appears in this option's content bullets. The third key topic names anti-Vietnam War protests, campaigns to improve welfare of the poor, Johnson's 'Great Society' and Nixon's pledges on welfare. Option A: keep the material as context for 'political, economic and social divisions' and for the key issue on support for and opposition to the state, since it sits inside 1945-1974. Option B: cut it back and retarget the practice question onto Nixon's welfare pledges. Recommend A, with no edit: the material is in period and serves a named key issue, and nothing in the lesson claims it is a listed topic.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md, content of the USA 1945-1974 depth study
findings.ruling: Leave: in-period context for the divisions key issue.

findings.claim: The Montgomery Bus Boycott is given as 381 days.
findings.truth: Counting 5 December 1955 to 20 December 1956 inclusive gives 382 days, which is what Wikipedia states; 381 is the figure in most GCSE textbooks and in the movement's own accounts. Recommend keeping 381 so the lesson matches the classroom books, and making no edit.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Montgomery bus boycott' vs standard GCSE textbooks
findings.ruling: Leave: 381 days is the textbook figure.

findings.claim: “By 1964, a decade after Brown, fewer than two per cent of Black students in the South attended desegregated schools.”
findings.truth: Published figures for 1964 range from about 1.2 per cent (eleven former Confederate states) to 2.3 per cent (the wider South). The claim sits inside that range, so it is defensible as written.
findings.evidence: Southern Education Reporting Service figures

findings.claim: “By 1968, an estimated 17 million Americans were boycotting grapes.”
findings.truth: The 17 million figure comes from a Harris poll usually dated 1969 or 1970. The number is right; the year may be a little early. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: Harris poll on the grape boycott

findings.claim: “bar patrons, including Marsha P. Johnson and other prominent figures, fought back”
findings.truth: Johnson herself said she arrived at the Stonewall Inn after the raid had begun, and none of those involved were prominent in June 1969. The sentence overstates a contested detail but does not misstate the event.
findings.evidence: Johnson's own account of the night

summary: Every lesson labelled its practice questions with question forms and marks from another board (4, 8 and 16-mark questions, 'Explain two reasons', a 'Depth Study Essay'), and the two-feature mark scheme awarded 4 marks for a 2-mark question; all nine sets were relabelled to the genuine 2 / 10 / 18-mark forms. Seven lessons also carried invented claims about what examiners reward. Content errors were few but real: the Welch quotation, the start and end dates of the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the white primary after 1944, the Selma broadcast, the exposure of COINTELPRO, AIM's founders, who organised the Alcatraz occupation, the date of the Cambodia announcement and Ford's pardon.
